The dedication of our volunteers and the financial contributions of cadet families cannot and must not become substitutes for adequate federal funding of the cadet program

— Jacquie Pepper-Journal, president of the Air Cadet League of Canada (CBC News)

Key Points

  • Public pressure: A Change.org petition calling for activities to resume drew more than 52,000 signatures, while Conservative and Bloc Québécois MPs raised the issue in the House of Commons [2][8].
  • Northern access: Cadet league leaders said the pause cancelled activities planned for Whitehorse, Yellowknife and Iqaluit, limiting opportunities for northern youth to travel and meet peers [6].
  • Local costs: The Army Cadet Corps in Yellowknife faced a $9,000 annual rent bill after Local Support Allocation funding was cut, even as weekly meetings continued [6].
  • Department-wide restraint: The Department of National Defence was expected to find $459 million in savings while prioritizing equipment purchases [3].

Perspectives

Department of National Defence: Vice-Admiral Angus Topshee said the department had to live within its means, despite the cadet program’s expanded budget [3].

Sources: CBC News

Air Cadet League of Canada: President Jacquie Pepper-Journal argued that the quality and accessibility of cadet programming should not depend on a community’s ability to raise money [6].

Sources: CBC News

Floyd Powder, Métis veteran and former cadet leader: Powder questioned whether southern-based decision-makers understood the effects of the activity restrictions in northern communities, where some young people have few alternatives [6].

Sources: CBC News

Timeline

  • 18 November 2026: The Ottawa Citizen reported that cadet training activities had been cut until at least April 2027 [5].
  • 20 November 2026: McGuinty said he had ordered a review of cadet funding reductions [9].
  • 23 November 2026: McGuinty announced additional funding to resume planned cadet activities [3][2].

Historical Background

A study funded by the Department of National Defence and completed in March found that each dollar spent on the cadet program generated an estimated $19.85 to $41.15 in lifetime social returns. It estimated lifetime net benefits to Canadian society of $295,600 to $630,500 per cadet and linked participation with educational, employment and civic outcomes [5].

Q&A

Q: Is funding guaranteed for the next fiscal year?

A: The Army, Navy and Air cadet leagues planned to meet with McGuinty before the holidays to seek clear answers on future funding [6].

item.content:encoded:
Bloc leader says Carney’s Trump roast risks worsening tariff tensions

Category: Canada

Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet criticized Prime Minister Mark Carney’s decision to bring an impersonator of U.S. President Donald Trump onstage at Ottawa’s annual Parliamentary Press Gallery dinner, calling the satire provocative and warning that U.S. tariffs are hurting Quebec’s aluminum sector [17]. The dinner is a political roast where politicians and journalists trade jokes; comedian Mark Critch portrayed Trump and Mark McKinney played Carney [11][7]. Canada and the United States continue trade negotiations. The impersonator joked that Trump himself was holding up a deal and mocked his handling of trade talks [13][7]. Blanchet said Quebec was paying a particularly high price for tariffs and argued the jokes should not inflame tensions [17]. Ottawa is seeking tariff relief in key sectors, including autos, but has warned that removing all U.S. tariffs is unlikely and that Canada may need to adjust to a changed trading relationship [17]. The dinner took place Saturday, Nov. 21, in Ottawa [21].

item.title: Scientists propose supercritical fluids drove deep Mariana volcanic eruptions
item.author: Kite Feed Generator (Science / Geology)
item.description: Researchers propose that supercritical water in magma could explain how volcanic deposits formed more than 6,000 meters down the Mariana Trench wall, building on the discovery of unusually deep pyroclastic rocks. At those pressures, water behaves neither like an ordinary liquid nor a gas and expands far less than steam. The team says this may have enabled magma to fragment without the force of a land eruption [9][6][1]. The mechanism remains uncertain: researchers have not found the vents or directly observed an eruption. Rock samples contain “double breccia,” suggesting two closely spaced episodes of fracturing — one possibly linked to supercritical fluid and another to its conversion to steam at the seafloor [9]. The team plans further analysis of the volcanic material and aims to explore farther along the plate boundary. Jason/Medea cannot descend below 6,500 meters, short of the Challenger Deep floor at about 11,000 meters [9][5].
item.content:encoded:
Scientists propose supercritical fluids drove deep Mariana volcanic eruptions

Category: Science

Researchers propose that supercritical water in magma could explain how volcanic deposits formed more than 6,000 meters down the Mariana Trench wall, building on the discovery of unusually deep pyroclastic rocks. At those pressures, water behaves neither like an ordinary liquid nor a gas and expands far less than steam. The team says this may have enabled magma to fragment without the force of a land eruption [9][6][1]. The mechanism remains uncertain: researchers have not found the vents or directly observed an eruption. Rock samples contain “double breccia,” suggesting two closely spaced episodes of fracturing — one possibly linked to supercritical fluid and another to its conversion to steam at the seafloor [9]. The team plans further analysis of the volcanic material and aims to explore farther along the plate boundary. Jason/Medea cannot descend below 6,500 meters, short of the Challenger Deep floor at about 11,000 meters [9][5].

Primary Source: View original article

Read more: Full article on Kite Static

What would explosive volcanism involving a supercritical fluid look like? How would that work? We’re at the limits of our intuition as geologists.

— Robert Stern, geoscientist at the University of Texas at Dallas (Physics World)

Did you know: The Shinkai Seep Field visited by the expedition is described as the deepest known hydrothermal vent field, where methane produced by seawater reacting with mantle rock supports life without sunlight [9].

Key Points

  • Flow route: The hot pyroclastic material moved downhill along the seabed rather than drifting through the water like ash, and likely did not travel far [1][9].
  • Seep field: The team recovered fluid-sampling devices that Japanese researchers had left at the site in 2016 [9][3].
  • Vent search: Because the flows moved downhill but did not travel far, researchers think the source may lie upslope of the deposits, on a ridge or the trench-facing slope [1].

Perspectives

Robert Stern, University of Texas at Dallas geoscientist and study leader: He called for investment in deep-sea research and technology to better understand supercritical fluids, which are also relevant to underground carbon capture and storage.

Sources: Physics World

David Pyle, volcanologist at the University of Oxford: He called the work a strong example of observational geoscience and suggested researchers investigate whether thermal shock or stresses from bubbles caused the rocks to fracture.

Sources: Physics World

Eoghan Reeves, aqueous geochemistry researcher at the University of Bergen: He said exceptionally deep, hotter vents could dissolve more metals and generate hydrogen that microbes use, though researchers have not found such vents at the site.

Sources: Physics World

Technical Details

  • Volcanic glass: Glass in the recovered rocks erodes quickly in seawater, suggesting the eruptions were geologically recent, although researchers are still dating the samples [4].
  • Deposit texture: The flows had lobed edges where they stopped, and the rock cracked into roughly rectangular blocks a few feet across as it cooled [1].

Scientific Significance

  • Forearc extension: Rock ages suggest the eastern segment is stretching mechanically while the western segment is accumulating magma; further sampling and radiometric dating are needed to test this interpretation [5].
  • Near-trench volcanism: The deposits lie about 100 kilometers from the trench, closer than typical volcanic arcs; a more steeply dipping Pacific plate could help explain that proximity [6].
  • Plate-motion implications: Researchers say stretching of the forearc means the subduction zone must widen, a change that could affect plate motions in the western Pacific [5].

Q&A

Q: Could eruptions still be happening there?

A: Researchers have proposed placing seismometers nearby to detect small earthquakes and help determine whether eruptions are continuing [1].

Q: Why was volcanism in this location unexpected?

A: The deposits are in a forearc where the mantle is generally considered too cool to melt, and the Challenger Deep segment lacks the organized volcanic arc found elsewhere along the Mariana Trench [4].

item.content:encoded:
Army says detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide in Iowa will proceed Wednesday

Category: Science

The U.S. Army plans to detonate 68 barrels of degraded lead azide at its ammunition plant near Middletown, Iowa, on Wednesday, Nov. 25, after a federal appeals court lifted a pause on the permit. Officials say the decades-old stockpile has become unstable and could explode even if left undisturbed as temperatures fall [16][20][14]. The three-judge panel found that environmental groups had not shown they were likely to succeed in their challenge and said the Environmental Protection Agency permit includes safeguards such as barriers, weather restrictions, advance notice and environmental monitoring [16][18]. President Trump had ordered the Army to wait for agreement from the court and Iowa’s governor-elect, Rob Sand. Sand said the administration should decide, and the Army later announced it would proceed [11][20][9]. The Army’s latest statement schedules the blast for Wednesday morning, citing forecast wind conditions. Farm Progress reported that plume maps are expected six hours before the detonation and hourly afterward [16][21].

Primary Source: View original article

Read more: Full article on Kite Static

But the Army created this emergency through neglect, and it owes the people of Iowa more information about the planned detonation and more safeguards for their health.

— Rachel Rintelmann, Earthjustice managing attorney (The Globe and Mail)

Key Points

  • Alternative review: The Army's records included chemical treatment and thermal options; a contracting officer told MuniRem the cancellation was not based on deficiencies in its science [18][3].
  • Public notice: Mediapolis Mayor Charles Massner told WIRED that an Army email in October gave no date, quantity or public-protection instructions, and that the town next heard about the imminent blast through a later Army release [3].

Perspectives

Rob Sand, Iowa governor-elect: Sand said Iowans should have access to the same information he received in federal briefings [20][14].

Sources: KXAN (Associated Press)

Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club: The groups argued that the permit failed to adequately assess the risks and alternatives to detonation [16][18].

Sources: The Globe and Mail

Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe: Kehoe stressed that Missouri, Iowa and Illinois had no say over when the federal operation would occur [20].

Sources: KXAN (Associated Press)

Timeline

  • March 2026: Army reported degraded lead azide and awarded a chemical-treatment contract [14][3]
  • 13 November 2026: EPA emergency permit authorizing controlled detonation took effect [14]
  • 19 November 2026: Environmental groups sued and appeals court temporarily stayed the permit [14][10]
  • 23 November 2026: Appeals court lifted its stay; Army announced Wednesday operation plans [16][20]

Technical Details

  • Recrystallized material: Army filings say liquid loss left crystals around the inside rims and undersides of drum lids; freezing can increase their sensitivity, and friction may initiate an explosive chain reaction [18][13].
  • Handling risk: The Army says chemical treatment requires opening or manipulating deteriorated containers, exposing personnel to friction and shock hazards over a prolonged period [7][14].

Industry Impact

  • Livestock and farming: Farm guidance recommends sheltering cattle with ventilation fans off and cleaning dust from stored outdoor hay before feeding, reflecting concerns about possible deposition on feed and animals [21].
  • Regional environmental monitoring: Illinois plans to use state air monitors and assess updated Army maps, while Missouri is preparing added air, water, public-health and agriculture monitoring [15][18].

Historical Background

A 2014 Army article said concern about a roughly 40-year-old stockpile of deteriorating lead azide at the Iowa facility had helped spur research into safer explosives in 2004 [5].

Travel Advisory

  • Safety: Officials advise people in potentially affected areas to remain indoors with windows closed during the event; Illinois guidance calls for staying inside for 24 to 48 hours afterward [15][17].
  • Cleanup: Officials recommend washing outdoor surfaces with water after the blast to limit contact with deposited particles [20][18]. Follow state and local cleanup instructions, and avoid disturbing dust until authorities provide updated guidance.

Q&A

Q: Does the governor-elect have legal authority to approve the blast?

A: Rob Sand does not take office until January, and reporting says his approval is not legally required; President Trump nevertheless made the operation subject to Sand’s agreement in his public statement [16][11].

Action Items

  • Check the latest Army plume maps and state or county alerts to determine whether your location is in the projected exposure area [21][20].

Umbra unveils Freetail 5 radar satellites with five-centimeter imaging

Category: Science

U.S. space technology company Umbra unveiled Freetail 5, a synthetic-aperture radar satellite model designed to produce images with resolution as fine as 5 centimeters. The first spacecraft is expected to launch in early 2028; Umbra says it will weigh about 200 kilograms and provide hourly global revisit capability [2][3]. Finnish satellite maker ICEYE is marketing its next-generation Gen5 radar spacecraft, which offers 11-centimeter imagery to government customers and 16-centimeter imagery to commercial customers. Commercial service is expected to begin in 2027 [3]. Radar can collect images through cloud cover that can hinder optical satellites, and governments in Europe are seeking sovereign Earth-imaging capabilities [3].

Time to decision is everything in space-based intelligence, whether you’re tracking a vessel or responding to a flood.

  • Expanded missions: Umbra says Freetail can support formation flight, single-pass 3D imaging, maritime search and direct-to-theater data downlink [2].
  • Radar upgrades: Umbra says Freetail 5 has four times the radar power and twice the antenna area of its previous spacecraft [2][3].
  • ICEYE approach: ICEYE plans to add an onboard artificial intelligence processor to screen and preprocess imagery in orbit rather than wait for data to reach the ground [3].

Umbra: CEO David Langan said the company is building a compact spacecraft to deliver the performance and mission flexibility of much larger systems for the United States and its allies.

item.title: November's Beaver supermoon peaks, beginning three consecutive supermoons
item.author: Kite Feed Generator (Science / Astronomy)
item.description: November’s Beaver Moon reached its full phase at 9:53 a.m. Eastern time Tuesday, Nov. 24, beginning a run of three consecutive supermoons, NASA says [5][4][2]. The full moon was about 224,170 miles from Earth; NASA planetary scientist Noah Petro said it appeared about 17% larger and 30% brighter than the year’s smallest full moon [6][2][8]. Because the peak occurred during daylight in North America, evening viewing offered the clearest chance to see it [6][1]. A supermoon occurs when a full moon is near perigee, the moon’s closest point to Earth in its orbit [6][5]. The size difference can be subtle to the eye, while the moon illusion can make the moon seem much larger when it is near the horizon [6][4]. December’s Cold Moon is next, reaching its peak on Dec. 23 [2][4].
item.content:encoded:
November's Beaver supermoon peaks, beginning three consecutive supermoons

Category: Science

November’s Beaver Moon reached its full phase at 9:53 a.m. Eastern time Tuesday, Nov. 24, beginning a run of three consecutive supermoons, NASA says [5][4][2]. The full moon was about 224,170 miles from Earth; NASA planetary scientist Noah Petro said it appeared about 17% larger and 30% brighter than the year’s smallest full moon [6][2][8]. Because the peak occurred during daylight in North America, evening viewing offered the clearest chance to see it [6][1].
